name: Insect screen
lede: Insect screen is a dark, muted green from Japan's traditional color list, and our own literal gloss of the name may be hiding a prettier story behind it.

sections.title: In Japan: Mushi'ao
sections.body:
The name is written 虫襖, romanized Mushi'ao, which our color library glosses literally as "insect screen" [1]. Japanese color-history sites instead tie this same name to the jewel beetle, or *tamamushi*: a dark, iridescent green said to echo the beetle's wing case, and treat Mushi'ao as effectively the same color as Tamamushi-iro, "jewel-beetle color" [2]. We cannot confirm which reading our own library's translation intends, so we give both [1][2].

The nearest named neighbor by measured color is [[shirvan]], with [[bakst-green]] close by, both almost the same shade [3]. [[nickle-green]] and [[dark-hunter-green]] sit a little further out [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a match for Insect screen in 391 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.64 percent, more common than 73 percent of the named colors we track, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 47 of 1,674 paintings from that century, 2.7 times the rate its share of the archive would predict [4]. Inside a painting it most often plays a shadow, in 41 percent of its appearances [4].

The painter most devoted to it is Harald Giersing, in 5 of his 23 paintings here, 8.4 times his peers' rate, as photographed [4]. The earliest archive match is dated 1400, in a work by Andrea di Bartolo; the archive's early centuries are thin, so that is a floor, not a first [4]. It shares canvases more than chance with the color we call Varley's Green [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications [4].
